objections.gloss: The larder books existence as a gift to the animal and spends that credit against everything done to her afterward. But a gift needs a recipient, and at the only moment existence could be conferred…
objections.title: These animals only exist because we breed them for food — no demand, no pigs at all. Give them decent lives and quick, unanticipated deaths and the practice has given them everything they have; a life worth living beats never existing. The pig has more stake in the demand for bacon than anyone. And death costs an animal little — no projects, no anticipation, only a weakly held future. Abolition wouldn't free a single one of them; it would make sure none is ever born again.

objections.gloss: Run the body count honestly and it inverts. Most cropland feeds livestock, so a calorie routed through an animal claims several times the acreage — and the field deaths — of the same calorie eaten…
objections.title: Spare me the clean-hands routine — your plate isn't bloodless either. The combine that brings in the soy and wheat minces field mice, voles, ground-nesting birds, rabbits by the million; pesticide poisons more; clearing habitat for monocrop starves out whole populations. A grass-fed steer, by contrast, lives on rough pasture that grows no crop and buries almost nothing under a blade, then feeds a family for a season. Do the arithmetic Steven Davis did: count the bodies per plate and the vegan's hands come out dirtier than the rancher's. If the whole case is harm-reduction, then least harm can mean eating the ruminant. You don't get to preach a body count you're losing.

objections.gloss: The objection concedes everything - victim, wrong, 'humane,' the vegan's own footprint - and stakes all on one claim: abstaining changes nothing. It fails twice, with a third hold that survives the…
objections.title: Grant it all. The animals count fully, the factory is a horror, 'humane' is a fig leaf, and yes - my own plate kills things in the fields too. I concede every inch. Here is the one inch I keep: my walking past the meat case changes nothing that happens to any animal. The chain moves in truckloads and case-lots, never single packs, and it keeps slack and stock precisely so that a few missing buyers never reach the order desk. My one forgone purchase is swallowed by the buffer - expected animals spared, near enough to zero to call it zero. A duty to perform an act that changes nothing is no duty. So grant that your ethics is flawless: it still lands on no one. It cannot reach me.

objections.gloss: The objection concedes the victim and the harm, then claims a warrant in nature: lions kill, meat is natural, nature needs no defence. But nature describes; it licenses nothing — and the objector…
objections.title: Lions eat gazelles. Predation is the oldest fact of nature; the food chain is not a moral failing. Humans are animals doing what animals do — eating meat is natural, and what is natural needs no defense.

objections.gloss: The objection concedes the harm and denies the victim — so everything rests on a property every human has and every animal lacks. None exists: a criterion strict enough to exclude animals…
objections.title: Animals aren't the kind of beings who can be wronged. Rights and wrongs hold between persons — rational, self-aware moral agents who can bear duties. Whatever eating meat is, it wrongs no one: there is no one there to wrong.

objections.gloss: 'Humane' is an adjective on one limb of the wrong. The charge here was never suffering alone - it was harm AND consent - and welfare buys off the first while the rest stands untouched. An animal kept…
objections.title: Don't lump me in with the factory - I'm against that as much as you are. But raise the animal properly: pasture, sun, a herd, the run of a full life, then one clean stroke it never sees coming. It didn't suffer. It had a good life and a painless death - a better deal than the wild would ever have cut it, where the ending is a torn throat or slow starvation. Cruelty is the crime, and I've taken the cruelty out. No pain in the living, none in the dying. So name the wrong that's left, because 'you killed it' isn't a wound when the dying cost it nothing at all.

objections.gloss: Two answers, and the second is fatal. First, the line is not 'animals because they resemble us' — it is valenced experience, which needs a substrate the plant has not got (nociceptors, a nervous…
objections.title: Plants are alive too — and don't tell me they don't feel it. Cut one and it floods the wound with chemicals; wound another and it signals its neighbours to arm up; Gagliano's peas even learned to expect a fan like Pavlov's dog. Electrical signalling runs the whole organism. So how are you so sure the wheat feels nothing while the pig feels everything? Draw the line honestly and you can't — 'animals in, plants out' is just a preference for creatures that look back at you. Either your suffering rule is arbitrary, or it convicts your salad too: every plate is a killing floor, and the only consistent vegan is a corpse. So climb down off the high ground — you eat the living, same as me.

objections.gloss: Dominion concedes the animal's interests and denies they bind, on grounds of rank: we are superior — more rational, more powerful, apex of the food chain, on one telling the appointed lords of…
objections.title: We aren't the animals' equals; we're their superiors. Scripture gives humankind dominion over the beasts — and even without it, we sit at the top: more rational, more powerful, the apex of the food chain. The lion doesn't apologise to the gazelle, and neither should we. Rank is real, and an inferior's interests were never a claim on a superior — being the lesser party, the animal was never owed a seat at the table.
